strengths: Well-motivated problem with strong statistical evidence (χ² test, p = 9.3×10^-15) of correlation between reasoning quality and code correctness
Comprehensive three-part framework systematically addressing benchmark construction, reward model training, and RL algorithm design
Strong empirical results achieving 4.5% improvement over outcome-only baselines and GPT-4-Turbo comparable performance across multiple benchmarks
Thorough experimental evaluation including ablation studies, reward hacking analysis, and generalization to mathematical tasks with public release of models/data
Clear presentation with informative figures and helpful qualitative examples demonstrating improved reasoning in code generation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: OD-based method is straightforward adaptation of EvolInstruct; posterior reward is simple gating mechanism; relies on established GRPO and Bradley-Terry approaches
Small benchmark (187 pairs) with multi-stage filtering that may introduce bias; reward model tied with GPT-4-Turbo on LCB-RB (58.28%), raising questions about benchmark discriminative value
Lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests; 4.5% improvement could be within noise margins; SFT baseline unexpectedly poor (66.2% vs 88.4%) without explanation

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: no validation that OD-based training outperforms score-based beyond citing insensitivity to numerical values; limited ablations on reasoning dimensions; only one qualitative example

Reward hacking analysis limited to 500 training steps; no empirical evidence that naive thinking reward integration exhibits exploitation; aggressive gating strategy (R_t=0 when R_o≠1) never ablated or justified

Design choices poorly justified: why use Qwen2.5-Coder-32B for score-based baseline rather than actual competitors; mismatch between GPT-4o validation and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B generation in LCB-RB construction
Limited scope: only 7B model evaluated; math experiments reuse code reward model without domain-specific justification; cross-domain generalization (7.4% improvement) weaker than code results
Potential data contamination not discussed; insufficient hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; reproducibility concerns regarding prompt wording sensitivity given extensive appendix prompts

strengths: Well-motivated problem with statistical evidence that reasoning quality correlates with code correctness; clear articulation of two key challenges (scarcity of preference data and reward hacking)
Novel CRPL approach elegantly addresses data scarcity through contrastive data synthesis rather than LLM-as-judge scoring, using targeted transformations along three reasoning dimensions
Principled consistency-gating mechanism (CG-GRPO) effectively prevents reward hacking; Figure 3(d) provides compelling evidence that process rewards inflate without gating while performance stagnates

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four benchmarks with strong results (16.1% relative improvement, comparable to GPT-4-Turbo on 7B model), thorough ablations, and cross-domain generalization
Rigorous benchmark construction with two-stage filtration addressing reasoning-implementation gaps; inter-annotator agreement κ=0.769 demonstrates reliability
Strong empirical findings on generation efficiency (23.4% fewer tokens with higher Pass@1) and complementarity with compiler-based supervision
Excellent reproducibility: public code and models, detailed implementation details, clear experimental setup
weaknesses: Synthetic data quality concerns: Single-generator training substantially outperforms cross-generator (11.0% improvement with 7B), suggesting reward model overfits to Qwen-specific degradation patterns rather than learning intrinsic reasoning quality; no validation that synthesized degradations match naturally-occurring errors

Limited scope of LCB-RB benchmark: Only 219 preference pairs with sparse valid rejected processes; random sampling for pair balancing could introduce bias; coverage of diverse reasoning failure modes unclear

Generalization claims overstated: Evaluation predominantly on Qwen2.5-7B with only brief Qwen3-4B test (400 steps vs 1,600); no evaluation on other model families (LLaMA, Mistral, etc.); RewardBench generalization claim relies on outcome-centric benchmarks, not reasoning-process centric

Experimental design questions: SFT baseline (39.1%) underperforms base model (50.4%) counterintuitively, unexplained; limited comparisons with related process-supervision methods (StepCoder, PRLCoder); missing error bars and statistical significance tests

Cost analysis absent: Computational cost of synthesizing with 32B model, training reward model, and RL inference not quantified or compared against alternatives; practical deployment implications unclear
Limited context length (4K tokens) insufficient for long-horizon reasoning exceeding 30K tokens; impact of context on reward quality not analyzed

Reward model calibration and sensitivity not thoroughly analyzed: Unclear if continuous scores are well-calibrated vs. learning rough preference orderings; no ablation on contribution of individual reasoning dimensions; potential distribution shift between training (Qwen-32B) and policy during RL not addressed

strengths: Well-motivated approach with strong empirical foundation (statistical validation in Appendix A.4 showing reasoning quality correlates with correctness, p<0.001)

Novel technical contributions: CRPL's targeted dimension-based synthesis is more principled than prior evolutionary strategies; CG-GRPO's consistency gate elegantly prevents reward hacking while preserving informative gradients among correct solutions
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 code benchmarks + 3 math benchmarks with strong baselines (GPT-4-Turbo, DeepSeek-V3); 16.1% relative improvement is substantial

Valuable benchmark contribution: LCB-RB with rigorous dual-validation (GPT-4o + human adjudication, κ=0.769) addressing reasoning-implementation gap; first benchmark for process-level reward discrimination in code
Strong cross-domain generalization to mathematics (7.4% improvement on AIME24); cross-model transfer to Qwen3-4B (11.1% improvement)

Thorough ablation studies demonstrating: (1) reward hacking vulnerability without gating (Figure 3d), (2) differential contribution of preference pair types (Figure 4), (3) complementarity with compiler-based supervision (Table 5)
Generation efficiency: achieves higher Pass@1 while generating 23.4% fewer tokens, suggesting gains from reasoning quality rather than increased compute
Rigorous methodology: clear problem decomposition, honest limitations section, promised artifact release, detailed hyperparameters and prompts in appendix
weaknesses: Context length constraint (4K max output) significantly limits applicability to complex reasoning problems requiring extended step-by-step derivations; acknowledged limitation but practically important
Limited scale of LCB-RB (219 pairs) constrains reward model evaluation; while manual verification improves quality, coverage and robustness unclear. No sensitivity analysis to dataset size variations

Synthetic data quality concerns: (1) Complete dependence on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B for meaningful optimization/degradation; (2) Inconsistent cross-generator results (Table 6: 3B model 11% worse, 7B model shows mixed results) suggest potential generator-specific overfitting rather than learning abstract reasoning quality; (3) No analysis of synthesis failure modes or cases where dimension-based perturbations fail to create meaningful distinctions

Missing statistical rigor: (1) No confidence intervals or significance tests on main results; (2) Some improvements modest (HumanEval+: 84.1%→86.0%, ~2.3% absolute); (3) Single run reported—variance across seeds unknown; (4) No computational cost-benefit analysis of reward model inference overhead
Scaling behavior largely unexplored: only evaluated on models up to 7B (with limited 4B results); behavior at 13B+ scales remains open question given increasing importance of larger models

Incomplete reward model evaluation: (1) 'Reasoning subset of RewardBench' undefined; (2) Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1 excluded from main results with minimal discussion despite being competitive; (3) Would benefit from additional held-out human evaluation of LCB-RB predictions at scale
Process-supervision baselines (StepCoder) underexplored: relegated to Table 5 with limited discussion; deserves more comprehensive comparison given complementary nature

Preference pair construction choices lack justification: (1) Equal weighting of three pair types despite Figure 4 showing differential contributions; (2) Why are Opt–Deg pairs 22.2% better? Could learned weighting improve efficiency? (3) No analysis of which problem categories benefit most from which pair types
Math domain results substantially smaller (7.4% vs. 16.1%) than code results—deeper analysis needed; only single model tested (Qwen2.5-Math-7B)
Missing key ablations: (1) Alternative loss functions (margin-based vs. Bradley-Terry); (2) Reward model size/architecture sensitivity; (3) Impact of individual filtering pipeline stages
